# Conversation Coach

Practise the conversations that matter before having them for real. Choose a scenario and difficulty, speak to an animated counterpart, and finish with two strengths, two improvements and a better way to phrase your response.

Built from the [Notion hackathon plan](https://app.notion.com/p/3f5d67cd0a05805b8023c53570998144). Scenarios: job interview, salary negotiation, relationship conversation, difficult feedback, and a custom scenario.

## Run locally

Use Node.js 22.21 or newer. Install with `npm ci`, copy `.env.example` to `.env.local`, then set `GEMINI_API_KEY` and `GRADIUM_API_KEY`. Run `npm run dev` and open http://127.0.0.1:3000.

Keys stay on the server. The page reports missing provider configuration; it does not substitute canned responses. `GEMINI_MODEL` defaults to `gemini-2.5-flash` from the supplied plan. Set it to a model available to your event account. `GRADIUM_VOICE_ID` defaults to the voice in Gradium's REST example; replace it with your Studio voice if needed. Google Cloud credits and Gemini API billing may differ: use credentials for the endpoint your event account provides.

## Demo

Select **Ask for a raise**, set the difficulty, and start practice. Give three short answers using the microphone or typed input. End the session to get feedback, then try again using the suggested phrasing.

The microphone uses push-to-talk: click to record, then finish your turn. Audio is encoded as actual mono PCM WAV, not WebM relabelled as WAV. Audio goes to Gradium; the transcript goes to Gemini; Gemini's reply goes to Gradium for spoken output. A typed turn skips transcription. The avatar has idle, listening, thinking and speaking states.

## Architecture and ownership

| Area | Files | Team responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rehearsal UI | `src/components/`, `src/app/` | Scenarios, avatar, transcript, feedback |
| Microphone | `src/hooks/`, `src/lib/audio.ts` | WAV capture and resource cleanup |
| Conversation | `src/lib/server/`, `src/app/api/converse/` | Gemini prompts and full history |
| Voice services | `src/app/api/transcribe/`, `src/app/api/speak/` | Gradium STT/TTS |
| Reliability | `src/**/*.test.ts`, `e2e/` | Contract, failure and browser checks |

The five-person team can own UI, microphone/voice, conversation/feedback, integration/deployment, and demo/testing separately. All use the shared contracts in `src/lib/contracts.ts`.

## API contracts

| Route | Request | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/status` | None | Provider key presence booleans; never keys |
| `POST /api/transcribe` | Raw `audio/wav` | `{ text }` |
| `POST /api/converse` | Session and message history | `{ reply }` |
| `POST /api/speak` | `{ text }` | `audio/wav` bytes |
| `POST /api/feedback` | Session and message history | `{ summary, strengths, improvements, suggestedResponse }` |

Session input: `scenarioId`, `difficulty`, optional `customScenario`, and `messages` containing `role` (`user` or `assistant`) and `content`. Scenario IDs: `interview`, `raise`, `relationship`, `feedback`, `custom`. Difficulties: `friendly`, `neutral`, `challenging`. Failures return `{ error }` with a non-200 status.

Transcripts live in browser memory only. The app does not save recordings, accounts or sessions. Feedback concerns the words spoken; it does not diagnose personality or mood. Provider retention policies still apply.

Requests are bounded to 64 KiB JSON, 40 messages, 4,000 characters per message and 24,000 characters total. Custom scenarios allow 1,500 characters; speech synthesis accepts 2,000. Recordings allow 60 seconds and 12 MiB, with provider calls limited to 25 seconds. The process-local limit is 60 POST requests per minute across all users; it is a demo safeguard, not a distributed production limiter. Deploying multiple replicas or opening the app publicly needs an appropriate access and usage policy.

## Validation

`npm test` runs unit and API integration tests with mocked providers. `npm run test:coverage` reports service and audio coverage. `npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint` and `npm run build` check the app. Install the test browser with `npx playwright install chromium`, then run `npm run test:e2e` for the browser flow. Mocked tests do not prove real credentials, quotas, microphone hardware or provider latency; validate those with a live three-turn rehearsal.

### Build evidence — 10 October 2026

The plan's journeys map to WAV encoding tests, mocked provider-route tests, and browser rehearsal tests. API and audio implementation used failing tests before implementation. A later browser regression reproduced the pending-microphone bug: `waiting for microphone permission cannot overlap a typed turn` failed because the composer was enabled. Locking microphone startup made that same test pass while reset remained available.

| Guarantee | Check | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Genuine PCM WAV, downsampling, bounded duration | `src/lib/audio.test.ts` | 6 tests pass |
| Full history, provider contracts, feedback shape, invalid inputs, safe failures | `src/lib/server/routes.test.ts` | 16 tests pass |
| Three-turn rehearsal, audio playback, feedback, reset, missing setup, speech failures, mobile layout, microphone startup race | `e2e/coach.spec.ts` | 7 tests pass |
| Type safety, lint, production compilation | `npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint`, `npm run build` | Pass |

`npm run test:coverage`: 95.16% statements and 91.12% branches in the instrumented service/audio scope. UI and recorder lifecycle are exercised by browser tests, not included in that percentage. `npm audit` after dependency setup and the final production-only audit reported zero vulnerabilities. Reviewer found no remaining blocking issue after the microphone fix. Live provider calls remain unverified because credentials were not configured. The worklet may omit the final partial 1,024-sample batch (up to about 21 ms at 48 kHz) when recording stops.

## Provider references

- [Google GenAI SDK / Gemini](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/generate-content)
- [Gradium STT REST](https://docs.gradium.ai/guides/speech-to-text-rest): raw WAV upload, NDJSON text segments
- [Gradium TTS REST](https://docs.gradium.ai/guides/text-to-speech-rest): WAV output with `only_audio: true`

Dependencies: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Lucide icons, Google GenAI, Zod. Validation: Vitest, Playwright, ESLint. The avatar is an original SVG implemented in the app.

- **Microphone and WAV encoding:** `src/hooks/use-voice-session.ts` and `src/lib/audio.ts`

- **Provider wrappers:** `src/lib/server/gemini.ts`, `gradium.ts`, plus validation and rate limiting
- **Tests:** Vitest unit/API tests with the providers mocked, and Playwright browser tests in `e2e/`

There are only two commits so far. The README says all tests pass but the app has never been tried with real API keys.

**Entire** (CLI v0.11.4, installed at `~/.local/bin/entire`) records your AI coding sessions and links them to your git commits. It's built into this repo in three places.

## How it hooks in

1. **Claude Code hooks** (`.claude/settings.json`): `entire` runs on session start and end, every prompt you submit, every time I stop, and on subagent and task events.
2. **Codex hooks** (`.codex/hooks.json`): the same idea for Codex. It also runs after **every** tool call.
3. **Git hooks** (`.git/hooks/`):
   - `prepare-commit-msg` / `commit-msg`: adds an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer to commit messages.
   - `post-commit`: packages the session data for commits that carry that trailer.
   - `post-rewrite`: keeps the session-to-commit links intact after an amend or rebase.
   - `pre-push`: per its own comment, "push session logs alongside user's push".

Every hook skips itself if `entire` isn't on your PATH, so teammates without it aren't blocked.

## What it can see

- **Your full Claude Code transcript.** The log points at `~/.claude/projects/.../<session>.jsonl`, and `.entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl` already holds a 267 KB copy of it. That copy includes your prompts, my replies and the output of every command I ran, including file contents.
- **Your latest prompt** (`prompt.txt`) and a snapshot of untracked files at the start of each turn (`.entire/tmp/`).
- **Your repo.** It sees which files changed during a turn so it can create checkpoints. My earlier turn changed nothing, so the log says "skipping checkpoint".
- **Your git commits and pushes**, through the git hooks above.

It **can't** see your keys or other secrets unless they end up in a transcript or get committed. When I checked your `.env` earlier I masked the values, so the stored transcript doesn't contain your keys.

## Where the data goes

- **Locally:** `.entire/metadata`, `logs` and `tmp` are gitignored, and telemetry is off (`"telemetry": false`).
- **Checkpoints:** these are stored as git refs (`"type": "git-refs"`). None exist yet, locally or on `origin`.
- **The remote:** when you `git push`, the pre-push hook can push the session logs as well. Your remote is `github.com/lambegraham/hackathon`, so your transcripts would become visible to anyone with access to that repo.

## Worth knowing

- **Redaction is not set up.** The log shows `active_rules:0, pii:false`, so nothing gets scrubbed from transcripts before they're stored or pushed. If you ever paste a key into a prompt, or have an agent print one, it would be stored and pushed as is.

Entire currently does two jobs in this repo. The recording side works on your machine. The Brain and Graph side doesn't yet.

## 1. Session recording (working)

`entire status` shows it enabled for **Claude Code and Codex**, with checkpoints syncing to `origin`. You're logged in as `github:anna-peter`, and your data is stored in the EU jurisdiction.

- **While an agent works:** the Claude and Codex hooks record each prompt, tool call and transcript. At the end of any turn that changed files, Entire saves a temporary checkpoint.
- **When you commit:** the git hooks add an `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer and turn the session into a permanent checkpoint linked to that commit. Your `3413b00` is one of these.
- **When you push:** the checkpoint refs go to GitHub under `refs/entire/checkpoints/*`. Graham's latest settings now have **`push_sessions: true`**. In my last message I said his settings had it set to `false`; he has since changed it. Every push now uploads full transcripts to the repo, so don't paste secrets into a prompt and don't let an agent print a key. Redaction is still not set up.

## 2. Brain and Graph (not working on your machine)

Graph is code search and impact analysis. Brain is shared team memory, where agents record durable facts and decisions and later get a "brief" built from them. Graham's commits connect these to the agents:

- `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` now pull in `.entire/agent-guide.md`. That file tells agents, including me, to start tasks with `entire brain brief "<task>"` and to save facts with `entire brain remember`.
- `.codex/config.toml` registers Brain as an MCP server for Codex. Nothing registers it for Claude Code yet.

On your machine neither command works: `entire brain` just prints the general help, `entire graph` hung until I stopped it, and `entire plugin list` shows no plugins installed. Graham probably has a plugin or a newer CLI that you don't. Ask him what he installed, or try `entire plugin search brain`. Until then, agents will skip that part of the guide.

## What you can do now

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `entire checkpoint list` | Checkpoints on this branch. You have 1 committed and 1 temporary. |
| `entire checkpoint explain <id\|commit>` | Explains what happened in a session or commit, e.g. `explain 3413b00` |
| `entire search "<query>"` | Searches across checkpoints, commits and sessions, including teammates' pushed sessions |

| `entire activity` | Your activity overview |
| `entire checkpoint tokens <id>` | Token usage per checkpoint |
| `entire doctor` | Fixes session problems. `status` warns that the merges may have thrown off attribution figures. |
| `entire configure` | Changes settings such as `push_sessions` or redaction |

For the hackathon, the most useful ones are probably `entire search` to find what a teammate's agent tried before, and `entire recap` for a quick summary of what the team did.

setup is the one command that makes a repository's brain useful and keeps it
that way. It runs three phases:

  1. instant   build the deterministic core (semantic index, sessions, seed,
               docs, history). Blocking, seconds, spends NO agent tokens. The
               brain is queryable the moment this returns.
  2. backfill  distill past sessions into durable facts, NEWEST FIRST, detached
               in the background on a cheap model. Spends tokens; bounded by
               --backfill-budget and the persisted distill cache, and skipped
               entirely when no agent CLI is available.
  3. daemon    register the repo into a workspace and install ONE machine-wide
               watcher service (launchd on macOS, a systemd user unit on Linux)
               so freshness never depends on remembering to run anything.
               ONE means one: the installed unit is identical for every repo and
               every workspace, and each workspace's interval, distill cadence,
               agent, model, effort and session cap live in a machine-level watch
               plan the running watcher re-reads. Setting up a second repo adds a
               row to that plan; it does not rewrite, restart or steal the
               watcher the first repo is relying on.

TOKEN SPEND: phases 2 and 3 call an agent. This is the first release in which
the watcher's --distill step and the session-end hook's distill actually run
(both were dead before), so setup is a real, recurring cost, bounded by four
gates: --backfill-budget sessions per background pass, one gated agent run per
--distill-every per repo, the persisted distill cache (a session is never
distilled twice), and the cheap --model/--effort. Passing --no-backfill with
--no-daemon spends nothing at all, and "entire brain status" reports what the
backfill has done so far and whether the watcher is alive.

content.text:
The voice tonality feature works and passed a live test with your real Gemini and Gradium keys. It's on a new branch, `feat/voice-tonality`, but nothing is committed or pushed yet.

**How it works**
- **Tone detection:** each conversation turn, Gemini classifies the tone of your latest message's wording as one of: confident, calm, enthusiastic, neutral, hesitant, nervous, defensive, frustrated or upset. Gemini then picks a matching tonality for its reply and writes the reply in that tone.
- **Voice choice:** Gradium has no tone setting on its speech API. Tone belongs to the voice itself, which is the "emotion" tag you see on Gradium's website. So each tonality maps to a real US-English voice, all checked against the live voice list: calm (Holly), reassuring (Hadley), empathic (Drew), friendly (Wendy), confident (Harrison), excited (Quinn) and neutral (Kelsey). You can swap any of them for your own voice with `GRADIUM_VOICE_CALM` and so on.
- **What you see:** a new "Their voice tone" picker offers "Auto · match my tone" or a fixed tone you choose. The stage shows a line like "You sound nervous → Alex answers reassuring · Hadley's voice", and each message in the transcript gets a small tone tag.
- **Tone is judged from the words only.** Gradium's transcription returns text, not how you sounded.

**Live results**
| Your message | Detected tone | Reply tone |
|---|---|---|
| "Um, sorry… talk about my pay?" | hesitant | reassuring |
| "I expect a 10 percent raise" | confident | neutral |
| "This is ridiculous…" | frustrated | calm |
| "I am so excited…" | enthusiastic | neutral |

All 7 voices returned valid audio in 1–1.6 seconds.

**Bug found and fixed:** Gemini 3.8 Flash spent almost all of its 500-token reply limit on internal thinking, which cut the reply off mid-sentence. The current code has the same problem, but there a cut-off sentence doesn't make the request fail. I set conversation turns to low thinking, and now each reply is about 50 tokens and complete. The feedback request still uses default thinking, and I haven't tested it live.

The voice tonality feature is committed, pushed to GitHub on `feat/voice-tonality`, and recorded in Entire.

**Commit and push**
- The commit is `81c2a88`, "feat: match counterpart voice tonality to the user's tone". It includes the feature, the tests, and a README section plus `.env.example` entries for the `GRADIUM_VOICE_<TONALITY>` overrides. I left out `next-env.d.ts`, which the dev server regenerates.

**Problem during the commit:** Entire's commit hook got stuck waiting for a confirmation that can't be shown when I commit, because it hides its output. I stopped the hook and the commit went through, but unlinked. Then `entire session attach --force` linked it before the push: checkpoint `01M4JZ2D1FCAG6P2FYN3D5XSN4` is now on the commit and was pushed with it. That checkpoint contains this whole session's transcript.

**Saved to Entire Brain** as 4 facts:
- Gradium has no tone setting, so tonality means choosing a voice, mapped in `src/lib/tonality.ts`.
- Gemini 3 counts thinking against the reply token limit, so conversation turns need low thinking.
- Only `GEMINI_MODEL` is read; `GEMINI_CONVERSATION_MODEL` and `GEMINI_FEEDBACK_MODEL` do nothing.
- How to fix the stuck commit hook when an agent commits.
